intro: Two models fit a small training set equally well but use very different weights. Add a penalty that makes weight size part of the objective, then trace exactly which gradients change.
task: Return loss, dw, and db for squared-error regression with an L2 weight penalty. Use loss = mean((X @ w + b - y)**2)/2 + strength * sum(w**2)/2. Do not penalize b.
requirements: X has nonempty shape (n,d), y has shape (n,), and w has shape (d,). b and strength are finite scalars; strength >= 0.
Return loss/db as numeric scalars and dw as a NumPy array. Reject malformed shapes and non-finite inputs with ValueError.
Average the data term over n. The penalty is not divided by n and applies to w only. This lesson fixes its own scaling convention.
Inputs must remain unchanged. Checks use moderate finite values.

hints.title: Separate the terms
hints.body: Compute the original regression loss and gradients first, then add the weight penalty.

hints.title: Differentiate the penalty
hints.body: The gradient of strength * sum(w**2)/2 with respect to w is strength*w. It contains no b.

hints.title: Check the convention
hints.body: Duplicating every training row should leave this objective and both gradients unchanged.

explanation: The data term rewards predictions that match targets. The second term charges for large weights, so even a perfect fit can have a nonzero objective and gradient.
For the stated convention, dw = X.T @ residual / n + strength*w, while db = mean(residual). The intercept does not appear in the penalty.
Penalty constants depend on whether a library sums or averages its data loss. Compare the full objective before transferring a strength value between implementations.

Experiment with a perfect fit and increase strength. Explain why a gradient step can temporarily increase training error while decreasing the regularized objective. Scale features using training statistics before comparing the cost of their coefficients.
